https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/a.text: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages GO Home World News Europe mulling culls for fish-guzzling cormorant AFP, PRAGUE Add TT as Preferred Source Europe’s great cormorant has recovered from near-extinction to overabundance in half a century, stoking a long-running debate over population control between fishers troubled by its voracious appetite and conservationists. The large black bird’s relentless raids on the continent’s waters have recently led nine EU members to urge an easing of the culling rules that have protected the species since 1979. “The situation is very bad and keeps worsening,” Peter Bozik from the Slovak Fishing Club said, calling the bird “a terrorist.” Czech Fishing Union ichthyologist Pavel Vrana poses with a taxidermy cormorant in Prague on Monday. Photo: AFP “When cormorants gather in wintering grounds, they can collect the entire fish population out of the unfrozen water in a moment, or damage it so that it will not survive,” he added. Czech Fishing Union ichthyologist Pavel Vrana said cormorants not only eat fish, but also often injure them or stress them out so they would not reproduce. “When you have 3,000 cormorants descending on a place, it’s a chainsaw massacre,” he said. Grigore Stefan, from the Murighiol Fishermen’s Association in the Danube Delta, said Romania lost “millions of fish” to cormorants annually. “It’s a harmful animal,” he said. “I don’t know if there are any fish left in the delta this summer.” In the past, Europeans systematically destroyed some cormorant colonies with the help of fire brigades and the military, a European Parliament report showed. Those efforts brought the species close to extinction. By the early 1960s, only a few thousand breeding pairs remained in the main breeding range of the Netherlands, Germany, Denmark, Sweden and Poland. However, since being granted protected status, its numbers have soared to an estimated 2 million in Europe this year. Czech Society for Ornithology head Zdenek Vermouzek said cormorants benefited from overfishing in the Baltic Sea, which has wiped out large predatory fish feeding on smaller fry. “The cormorants have simply replaced these predators,” he said. In central Europe, fish lack hiding places, as authorities are quick to clear natural shelters such as fallen trees, while ponds resemble “fish tubs” with steep banks, making them vulnerable to predators, Vermouzek added. Romania’s General Association of Hunters and Sport Fishermen said cormorants also have “very few natural predators and so multiply uncontrollably.” Vrana proposed oiling eggs in the nest to close the pores through which the embryo breathes as an efficient culling method. “If we want to ecologically and efficiently curb the population, it must happen in the place where they reproduce, no matter how terrible that sounds,” he said. Conservationists disagree, although they accept the practice of shooting cormorants to deter them from areas where fish winter. Vermouzek was skeptical of large-scale measures for which “we don’t have the men and we don’t have the guns.” Instead, he proposed reducing river-clearing operations to give fish better hiding places from the birds and returning to nature-driven management on the region’s exposed ponds. Conservationists and fishers agree humanity is to blame for the damage, but while environmentalists favor letting nature run its course, fishers want greater human intervention. “If mankind has erred, mankind must make amends. We cannot rely on natural mechanisms at a time when nature’s hands are tied,” Vrana said. https://www.thevermilion.com/a-drone-exp.text: A drone exploded near the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline between Bulgaria and Romania: “Vital for Ukraine” A drone exploded in Bulgarian territory not far from the border with Romania and one of the most important energy infrastructures in south-eastern Europe. The episode occurred on 8 August 2026 in the Kardam area, … Written by: Jack Williams Published on: August 8, 2026 A drone exploded in Bulgarian territory not far from the border with Romania and one of the most important energy infrastructures in south-eastern Europe. The episode occurred on 8 August 2026 in the Kardam area, in north-eastern Bulgaria, near the Black Sea. There were no victims or damage to infrastructure, but the proximity to the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline makes the incident particularly delicate. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev reported that the drone fell and exploded about one hundred meters inside the national territory, in a sunflower field, about a kilometer from the compressor station connected to the Trans-Balkan system. Bulgarian authorities are examining the remains of the aircraft. At the moment its origin has not been disclosed and there is insufficient public evidence to attribute it to Russia, Ukraine or other entities. Did the drone come from Romania? According to the reconstruction provided by the Bulgarian authorities, the drone came from the direction of Romania. The unidentified aircraft would not have appeared on the Romanian and Bulgarian radar systems nor would it have been detected by the NATO systems that monitor the area a stone’s throw from Negru Vodă, one of the points through which the gas networks of Romania and Bulgaria are connected. What is the Transbalkan pipeline As mentioned, the point is particularly delicate due to the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, an infrastructure built to transport Soviet gas to the Balkans via Ukraine, Moldova, Romania, Bulgaria and finally Turkey with connections also to Greece and North Macedonia. In Romania one of the main routes crosses the country from Isaccea, near the Ukrainian border, to Negru Vodă. From here the pipelines cross the border into Bulgaria right in the Kardam area, where the drone explosion occurred. For decades this corridor was one of the main gateways through which Russian gas reached Türkiye and the Balkans. However, now that European energy balances have changed profoundly, also thanks to the construction of TurkStream, which brings Russian gas directly from Russia to Turkey crossing the Black Sea, an important part of the old Transbalkan has lost its original function. The networks were therefore progressively adapted to allow the gas to also travel in the reverse direction, restoring strategic importance to the infrastructure after the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the progressive reduction of European dependence on Russian gas. In fact, supplies from various sources can travel northwards through the Balkan network: Azerbaijani gas, liquefied natural gas arriving at terminals in Greece, supplies sent through Turkey and, in the future, a growing quantity of gas extracted in the Black Sea. Why the Trans-Balkan is important for Ukraine Ukraine’s position in the European gas market has changed dramatically in recent years. For decades Kiev was above all the large transit country used by Russia to bring its gas to the European Union. With the reduction and then interruption of most of these flows, Ukraine has instead needed to strengthen the routes through which it can import gas from Europe. The Transbalkan offers one such alternative. In 2025, Ukraine also used the corridor to import gas from Azerbaijan for the first time, via a route that passes through Bulgaria and Romania before reaching Ukrainian territory. The explosion one kilometer from the gas station This is what makes the position in which the drone fell significant. Kardam is not just a small border town between Bulgaria and Romania. It is one of the focal points of the energy system that connects the networks of the two countries and, through them, the Black Sea and the Balkans with Moldova and Ukraine. According to information communicated by the Bulgarian government, the drone exploded about one kilometer from the Transbalkan compressor station. There is no damage to the structure and there are, at present, no elements that allow us to claim that the gas pipeline was the target of the aircraft. The geographical coincidence, however, remains relevant: the accident occurred next to an infrastructure which, created to bring Russian gas to Turkey, has become one of the possible alternative energy routes through which Ukraine can receive supplies from south-eastern Europe. Photograph: Kim Shapley/Alamy Tasmania More than 150,000 underwater explosives used to deter seals at Tasmanian salmon farms since 2016 Salmon companies operating in Tasmanian marine areas deployed almost 1,800 explosives in first half of 2026, government figures reveal Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Bob Burton Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 150,000 underwater explosives have been used to deter seals at Tasmanian salmon farms since 2016, according to new government data. Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE Tas) data released last week revealed salmon companies directed almost 1,800 underwater explosives at seals at fish farms in the first half of 2026. Since the start of 2016, the three salmon companies operating in Tasmanian marine areas – Huon Aquaculture, Tassal and Petuna – have deployed 150,488 underwater explosives. Four fur seals died in the first half of 2026 – two at Tassal leases and two at Huon Aquaculture sites. Two died entangled at salmon cages, one from a boat strike and another in an attempt to sedate and relocate an animal. Since the start of 2021, 48 seals have died at Tasmanian salmon farms. The use of underwater explosives against seals has declined sharply since April 2021, possibly in response to the publication of Richard Flanagan ’s book Toxic . Since early 2022, NRE Tas has released biannual data, with a company-by-company and month-by-month breakdown of the use of devices against seals, after a right-to-information request by the Tasmanian Inquirer . Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Huon Aquaculture, owned by the Brazilian meat company JBS, accounted for 1,126 of the explosives used in the first half of 2026, almost two-thirds of the total. Of these, 892 were used at the company’s leases in Storm Bay off the coast of Bruny Island, with the remainder at sites in the D’Entrecasteaux Channel and Huon River. Huon is now the largest salmon producer in the state, according to an analysis of government production data published by SalmonBusiness . After rotting salmon flesh washed up on beaches in the D’Entrecasteaux Channel in early 2025, and incidents of mass deaths at fish farms over the past two years, the company launched a PR blitz, including a video featuring seals swimming in the ocean. Tassal’s 2025 sustainability report said the company aimed to “phase out” the use of seal deterrents, but did not specify a deadline. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Tasmanian salmon farms blocked from using antibiotic florfenicol after detection in wild fish 10km away Read more Huon was asked whether it had a policy to phase out deterrents, and whether the high level of underwater explosive use against seals at the Storm Bay leases indicated the cages there were more prone to breakage due to exposure to rougher conditions. The company did not respond to these specific questions, but a Huon spokesperson said the company took its responsibility to protect wildlife seriously and was evaluating initiatives to improve wildlife safety. “This includes upgrades to existing infrastructure, adoption of new technologies to deter wildlife, and engagement with specialist consultants to assess and reduce interaction risks,” the spokesperson said. In its sustainability report, Tassal reported that seals gained access to salmon cages 1,100 times in the past three years. It said there was a 26% fall in seals getting into cages in 2025 compared with the previous year. But the company’s use of explosives against seals has begun rising again after four years of decline. In the first half of 2026, it used 551 explosive devices, more than double the number in the same period in either of the two preceding years. More than half of these devices were used at leases on the Tasman Peninsula. Tassal also used 31 bean bag rounds – fabric-coated plastic shells containing lead shot – against seals at its leases on the Tasman Peninsula. Tassal is the only salmon company that uses these devices in Tasmania. Tassal was asked whether its increased use of explosives at its Tasman Peninsula leases was due to the seal population near Nubeena growing, and whether the company had an end date for using devices against seals. Tassal, which is owned by Canadian multinational Cooke Aquaculture, did not respond. Petuna, the smallest of the state’s three marine salmon producers, used 82 underwater explosives against seals at leases in Macquarie Harbour and 38 at leases in the Tamar River. https://www.politico.eu/article/afd-alic.text: Far-right Alternative for Germany leader Alice Weidel told European lawmakers on Wednesday that Russia and Ukraine need to negotiate a peace deal, while insisting that German businesses require access to cheap Russian energy to remain competitive. “It isn’t about capitulating to Russia, far from it, absolutely not, but we want people to sit down around the table. It’s high time they did, and went into it with a sensible diplomatic approach, making sure we pay due regard to the interests of both Ukraine and Russia,” she told a press conference. Four and a half years since Russia launched its war on Ukraine, President Donald Trump is pressing Kyiv to negotiate with Moscow, while Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed on Wednesday to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine. Advertisement Advertisement Weidel made the comments during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, where she unveiled her opposition AfD party’s EU program at an event organized by the far-right Europe of Sovereign Nations group. The party aims to shrink the Commission, turn the European Parliament into an assembly of delegates appointed by national parliaments, and seek an opt-out for Germany from EU policies it can’t reform to its liking — potentially including an exit from the Schengen border-free travel area, she told reporters. During an event following the press conference, Polish MEP Tobiasz Bocheński from the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists group asked what she thought of Poland’s fears regarding Russia. Weidel said her party “puts German interests first,” insisting that “now we are in a critical phase that our industry is dying without Russian gas and oil . ” Germany needs “a sustainable, reliable and cheap energy resource that has been guaranteed by Russia for the last four decades,” she added, claiming that sanctions on Russia have “destroyed” Germany’s “business model.” German industry is shedding jobs amid high energy costs, Chinese competition and U.S. tariffs, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz continues to push for reforms to revive a stagnant economy. Weidel said that Russia, the U.S. and China are the only ones steering talks on Ukraine while European leaders aren’t even invited to sit at the table. The EU should have pushed for peace since the start, she added, as “four years down the road, it’s in a much worse position going into negotiations with Russia.” Advertisement Advertisement EU countries are discussing who should represent them at the negotiating table. European leaders have repeatedly said that any decision on a peace deal must involve Ukraine and must include security guarantees. Asked whether she was in contact with France’s far-right National Rally to repair ties, Weidel said the AfD was “pragmatic.” The French party broke with the AfD in 2024 and later helped shut it out of the far-right Patriots group amid concerns about its extremism and stance on Russia. “We need to work together on a European unique level, and therefore we need to be in talks and discussions,” Weidel said, adding: “And we are.”
